name: traversal-placement-value-create-payload
description: The SECOND client value that reaches a path component: `swc.group`, which is placement metadata and is persisted as the element's directory. The address is impeccable — `{layer: swc, element: SpeedSensorSWC}`, a legal identity — and the traversal is in the PAYLOAD, where `$defs/identity` cannot reach it. The no-traversal rule covers both values; this is the vector for the one that has no envelope guard.

context.summary: The `examples/basic` model. `SpeedSensorSWC` does not exist, so nothing about this change set is a collision; the only thing wrong with it is where it asks the component to be stored.

authorization.notes: The scope covers the requested operation exactly, so the refusal is about the placement value and not about authorization. A scope can never authorize a traversal: the guard is not an authorization question.

value.name: SpeedSensorSWC
value.description: Reads the wheel speed sensors and publishes the vehicle speed

expected.notes: `semantic` and not `protocol-schema`: `protocol.schema.json` deliberately does not restate `schema.py`, and a create payload is an open object there — so the envelope admits this request and the registry is what refuses the value. The same code the element identity gets one layer up, which is the point: the two values the no-traversal rule covers answer the same way, at the field the client wrote, and neither is sanitized into a legal one. The rejection happens at BIND time, so nothing is staged, no file is composed and the model stays byte-identical; a `change_set_rejected` record is still written, because a refused change set still happened.
